transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-02-24 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Robin Patel (Redwood SA), Priya Singh (CTO - Northhaven), Marcelo Ruiz (Head of MLOps), Anika Verma (SRE lead), Samir Patel (Product)

--- Optional autogenerated summary (may be imperfect) ---
Auto-Summary: Northhaven is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for predictable inference billing and isolation for PII scoring. They have two regulated flows that must remain in a private VPC or on-prem. Primary ask — how to guarantee burst capacity for event-driven spikes while keeping 99th percentile latency under 250ms for small gen tasks; also want fallback strategy if reserved pool saturated.

00:00 Laura Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. Quick round robin, who do we have on the call?
00:08 Priya Singh: Hi Priya here, CTO at Northhaven. Marcelo and Anika from infra are on as well. Samir in product.
00:12 Marcelo Ruiz: Marcelo, hey.
00:13 Anika Verma: Anika, SRE.
00:15 Laura Chen: Great, I'm Laura, AE, and I have Diego and Robin from our technical team. We'll keep this focused on reserved capacity and burst/fallback, yeah?
00:22 Priya Singh: Yes that's right. We're trying to decide between Redwood Hosted and Dedicated. For most of our customers we need data isolation and audit logs, and we also want predictable latency for our scoring pipeline.
00:31 Diego Morales: Cool. Can you walk me through the workload profile — batch vs real time, token lengths, peak qps, that sort of thing? If you have any sample traces even rough numbers that helps.
00:40 Marcelo Ruiz: Sure. Two main flows: realtime scoring for customer-facing features, small prompts, about 50-300 tokens, target p95 < 250ms, typical baseline 120 rps, peaks up to 450 rps for 10-15 minute bursts (campaign-driven spikes). Second is nightly batch rerank — large batches, throughput matters more than latency.
01:02 Robin Patel: And where is your data today? Is it cloud-only, any requirements around residency or air-gap?
01:07 Priya Singh: Mostly cloud, but a subset of our enterprise customers require a private deployment inside their VPC or even on-prem. For those we'd need private control plane or on-prem installer. That's one reason Dedicated is interesting.
01:18 Laura Chen: Understood. A couple of quick clarifying questions: Do the enterprise customers require full on-prem inference or is VPC-only acceptable? And are the sensitive requests the realtime path or also batch?
01:28 Priya Singh: For at least two customers it's VPC-only with company-managed keys; one has expressed that they might require an air-gapped appliance later — that's why we want options. And it's mainly realtime requests that are sensitive. Batch can be tokenized and scrubbed.
01:41 Diego Morales: For VPC we can run our private control plane so telemetry doesn't leave their VPC; KMS/HSM integration is supported. Our Dedicated offering can also reserve physical GPUs per customer or per account depending on tenancy needs.
01:55 Marcelo Ruiz: When you say "reserve physical GPUs" do you mean single-tenant hardware or logical isolation? We need to understand blast radius.
02:03 Robin Patel: We offer a couple of tenancy models — full node reservation (single-tenant) vs isolated tenant slices on dedicated pools with cgroup isolation. Single-tenant nodes are the strictest for blast radius, there's a premium.
02:17 Samir Patel: How does bursting work though? If we reserve 4 nodes for baseline but then get a spike where traffic triples, can you burst beyond reservation?
02:26 Laura Chen: Yes, we support configurable burst capacity. Two levers: pre-warmed hotpool for short spikes and on-demand burst into a shared spot-like pool with limits. The hotpool is best for short spikes where latency matters; the shared pool is lower priority and may have higher cold-starts.
02:43 Priya Singh: What's the SLA behavior when the reserved pool is exhausted and you route to the shared pool? We cannot have unpredictable P99s for our realtime lane.
02:51 Diego Morales: Good question. We recommend a tiered fallback: 1) prewarm hotpool sized for expected X-minute bursts (we do prefix caching and KV cash — sorry KV cache — to speed up continuation responses), 2) fallback to a compatible smaller model variant that meets latency, 3) degrade noncritical requests or queue with graceful retry. We have routing policies to prefer reserved nodes and there are controls to set hard limits per route.
03:18 Anika Verma: That fallback to a smaller model concerns product quality — if we degrade model size, outputs differ and downstream features may break. We need canary testing and metric alerting for quality regressions.
03:28 Diego Morales: Absolutely. We integrate with Redwood Optimize to run prompt evals and quality monitoring so you can tie regressions to rollout. Canary traffic can be routed to the alternate model so you can validate.
03:38 Marcelo Ruiz: For prewarming, is there an ongoing cost? If we keep hotpool nodes up 24/7 that's expensive. We want a cost model for committed baseline plus short warm bursts.
03:47 Laura Chen: Yep cost tiers: reserved nodes have monthly commitment; hotpool prewarm is either included as a small cushion in the reserved contract or billed as short-duration usage depending on how you set the policy. We'll include sample amortized numbers in the pricing worksheet.
03:59 Priya Singh: One thing we worry about — noisy neighbor or firmware-level preemption on shared infra. If another tenant triggers heavy ops and preempts resources, will we be impacted?
04:10 Robin Patel: For dedicated pools that are single-tenant there's no sharing. For mixed dedicated pools with tenant slices we use strict resource isolation; preemption is avoided by reserved capacity policies. If you need maximum control, single-tenant nodes are the path.
04:23 Samir Patel: Operationally, what does the rollout look like — how do we migrate customers gradually?
04:28 Laura Chen: Typical pattern: start with non-sensitive customers on Hosted to validate model behavior, then pilot Dedicated for a subset of customers (canary), then cutover sensitive customers once metrics look stable. We provide A/B routing, canary windows, and rollback policies.
04:40 Priya Singh: Regarding metrics, we need token-level cost breakdowns and traces at route level. Can we integrate with our existing observability stack?
04:47 Diego Morales: Yes we expose traces, per-route latency breakdowns, token cost estimates, and can forward logs to your Splunk/Datadog or push wire events to an S3 bucket. Audit logs and fine-grained RBAC are supported.
04:59 Marcelo Ruiz: Let's talk numbers — what's realistic to provision for our baseline 120 rps and peaks to 450 rps? We ran preliminary perf tests internally but the numbers vary with sequence length and model.
05:11 Robin Patel: If your median request is 150 tokens and you're using a 7B-class model quantized, rough thumb rule: one A100-style GPU can sustain ~200-300 small-generation rps with batching; for low latency targets we lean towards more nodes with smaller batch windows. For 120 rps baseline and 450 rps peaks, I'd propose a reserved pool sized for baseline + a hotpool sized for typical bursts (e.g., 2-3 extra nodes) and a burst path to scale further for rare events.
05:38 Marcelo Ruiz: That mapping helps. Can you provide a variant for different model classes? We have some customers using larger 65B for high-quality text and others happy with smaller distilled models.
05:47 Diego Morales: We'll prepare a sizing table across model classes (7B/13B/65B) including token/s cost estimates. For the big models the CPU/GPU memory shape changes the effective rps and cold start behavior.
05:58 Priya Singh: On security: we need SSO, SAML, SCIM, audit trails, and support for customer-managed KMS with HSM keys. Also a compliance package for financial regs.
06:10 Laura Chen: We have SSO, SAML, SCIM and support KMIP/KMS integrations. For compliance we share SOC2, and we have an enterprise package for extended retention and audit attestation. We'll attach the security pack docs.
06:21 Anika Verma: For private control plane, how does patching and updates work? We can't accept automatic updates for some enterprise instances.
06:28 Robin Patel: On the private control plane and on-prem installer we support a maintenance window model. Updates are scheduled with customer approval. For on-prem air-gapped, we provide patch bundles and a documented upgrade path.
06:39 Samir Patel: A question on pricing: is there a difference in contract terms or lead time for single-tenant nodes?
06:46 Laura Chen: Yes single-tenant physical nodes require lead time for procurement and capacity reservation; contract terms have a higher minimum and a longer commit window. We'll show lead times and cost deltas in the pricing sheet.
06:57 Marcelo Ruiz: What's your observability retention? We need 90 days by default for route-level traces.
07:03 Diego Morales: Base retention is 30 days; enterprise add-ons can extend to 90 or more. We'll include that option and cost.
07:09 Priya Singh: For routing policies, can we do region-based fallback? Some customers have residency constraints, so if a region is saturated we need to failover to a different region within the same jurisdiction.
07:20 Robin Patel: Yes. We support region-aware routing policies and can define a region priority list. In constrained cases we can failover to a compatible model hosted in the approved region only.
07:29 Anika Verma: About telemetry — is there a way to get token-level costs per customer in near real-time for chargebacks?
07:36 Diego Morales: We expose per-tenant token accounting with a lag of a few minutes and hooks to stream usage to your billing system for chargebacks.
07:43 Priya Singh: We run internal chaos tests. If a reserved node goes down, what's the expected RTO with your Dedicated model?
07:51 Robin Patel: RTO varies by redundancy. With multi-node reservation and autoscaling fallback, typical failover for stateless requests is sub-30s to route to another node; KV cache warmup may take longer. For strict RTO you want a hotpool sized to cover your critical requests.
08:06 Marcelo Ruiz: Do you perform automatic model fallbacks or is that something we configure?
08:12 Diego Morales: We provide the mechanisms and default policies; you can configure per-route fallback actions (model variant, queue, shed). We'll pair during the pilot to tune them.
08:21 Priya Singh: OK, couple of concerns from legal: data retention of request logs, encryption at rest, and subprocessor lists. We'll need that for procurement.
08:31 Laura Chen: We'll attach the data processing addendum, subprocessor list, and retention options. Procurement typically needs those before signature.
08:36 Samir Patel: Is there a straightforward on-prem PoC path? We could trial one of our customers with an on-prem installer for a two-week pilot.
08:44 Robin Patel: Yes we can do an on-prem pilot. For air-gapped installs we require lead time and discrete engineer support. We'll put an SOW for a 2-week pilot and include an engineer to help.
08:55 Marcelo Ruiz: Let's close the loop on the sizing: Marcelo will share traffic histograms, and Robin will turn that into a proposed reserved+hotpool plan.
09:03 Laura Chen: Great. Any last questions?
09:06 Priya Singh: One more — SLA credits and support escalation paths. We need clear escalation and an account manager plus a named support engineer for the Dedicated contract.
09:16 Laura Chen: Enterprise accounts get an assigned CSM and a dedicated support contact with faster SLAs. We'll include support tiers in the quote.
09:22 Anika Verma: Also want a runbook for operations playbooks — how to perform an emergency scale or graceful degrade.
09:29 Diego Morales: We'll provide our default runbook and we can co-author a joint runbook for Northhaven's processes during the pilot.
09:35 Priya Singh: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
09:37 Laura Chen: Thanks Priya. We'll follow up with the pricing worksheet, security artifacts, and propose deep-dive slots. Expect the pricing and security docs by EOD Friday.
09:46 End meeting
